t.5.1.1: Then the tormentor of his foes resolved to search out the trace of Sītā, who had been carried off by Rāvaṇa, along the path frequented by the Cāraṇas.
t.5.1.3: Terrifying the birds, sweeping away the trees with his chest and striking down a great many beasts, the wise one moved on like a full-grown lion.
t.5.1.2: Then the mighty and steadfast one roamed at his ease over grassy meadows the colour of beryl, which seemed like expanses of water.
t.5.1.5: It was constantly frequented by Yakṣas, Kiṃnaras and Gandharvas, who could take on any form at will, together with their retinues, and by godlike serpents.
t.5.1.4: It was richly adorned with many-hued minerals, formed by nature itself, of blue, red, madder and lotus colours, both white and black.
t.5.1.7: Having made a respectful añjali to Sūrya, to the great Indra, to Pavana, to Svayambhū, and to all beings, he set his mind upon departing.
t.5.1.6: Standing there on the slopes of that foremost of mountains, which teemed with excellent elephants, the best of monkeys shone like an elephant in a lake.
t.5.1.8: Facing east and joining his palms in reverence to Pavana, the source of his own being, the skillful one then grew in size so that he might go toward the southern direction.
t.5.1.9: Watched by the foremost of the monkeys, he who had resolved upon the leap grew in size for the furtherance of Rāma's cause, like the ocean swelling at the moon's changes.
t.5.1.10: Being of immeasurable body and eager to leap across the ocean, he pressed down upon the mountain with his two arms and his two feet.
t.5.1.12: Covered on every side by that fragrant mass of flowers released by the trees, the mountain shone as though it were made of flowers.
t.5.1.11: Pressed down by the monkey, the mountain shook for a moment, and the hills swayed charmingly; it shed all the blossoms from the trees whose crowns were in flower.
t.5.1.13: And that mountain, pressed down by him of supreme might, poured forth streams of water, as an elephant in rut pours forth its ichor.
t.5.1.15: As the mountain was being pressed down, the creatures that had entered its caves, crushed on every side, cried out with distorted voices.
t.5.1.14: Pressed by that mighty one, Mount Mahendra sent forth streams of gold, collyrium and silver, and the mountain cast off huge rocks streaked with red arsenic.
t.5.1.16: That great clamour of the mighty creatures, born of the crushing of the mountain, filled the earth, the directions, and the groves.
t.5.1.17: Serpents with broad heads bearing clearly visible svastika marks, vomiting terrible fire, bit the rocks with their fangs.
t.5.1.18: Then those great rocks, bitten by those enraged venomous serpents, blazed up as if kindled by fire and shattered into a thousand pieces.
t.5.1.19: And the clusters of medicinal herbs that grew on that mountain, though they were antidotes to poison, could not quell the venom of the serpents.
t.5.1.20: Thinking, “This mountain is being split apart by spirits,” the ascetics and the terrified Vidyādharas flew up from it together with their bands of women.
t.5.1.21: Leaving behind the golden seats and vessels that lay in the drinking-ground, the costly cups and the golden water-jars,
t.5.1.22: Lickable delicacies and foods of every kind, diverse meats, shields of bull's hide, and swords with golden hilts.
t.5.1.24: Women wearing necklaces, anklets, armlets and bracelets stood in the sky together with their lovers, astonished and smiling.
t.5.1.23: Wearing ornaments about their throats, intoxicated, adorned with red garlands and red unguents, red-eyed and lotus-eyed, they rose up into the sky.
t.5.1.25: Displaying their great magical knowledge, the Vidyādharas and the great sages stood together in the sky and gazed upon the mountain.
t.5.1.26: And then they heard the voice of the sages of purified souls, and of the Cāraṇas and Siddhas, who were stationed in the spotless sky.
t.5.1.27: This Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, who resembles a mountain, wishes to cross the ocean of great swiftness, the abode of makaras.
t.5.1.28: Wishing to accomplish a difficult deed for the sake of Rāma and for the sake of the monkeys, he desires to reach the far shore of the ocean, so hard to attain.
t.5.1.29: He, who was like a mountain, shook out the hair of his body and trembled, and he roared a mighty roar like a vast rain-cloud.
t.5.1.31: The tail of that exceedingly swift one, raised and lashing behind him, appeared like a great serpent being carried off by Garuḍa.
t.5.1.32: He braced his two arms, which resembled great iron bars, and the monkey sank down at the waist and drew in his feet.
t.5.1.30: About to leap up, he flung out his tail, rounded, tapering by degrees and covered with hair, just as the king of birds flings a serpent.
t.5.1.34: Surveying the path from afar, his eyes fixed upward, he held his breath within his heart as he gazed at the sky.
t.5.1.33: Drawing in his arms and likewise his neck, the glorious and mighty one entered fully into his splendor, his courage and his strength.
t.5.1.35: Planting himself firmly on his two feet and laying back his ears, that elephant among monkeys, the mighty Hanumān, best of monkeys, about to leap into the sky, spoke these words to the monkeys.
t.5.1.36: Just as an arrow released by Rāghava would fly with the speed of the wind, so shall I go to Laṅkā, which is guarded by Rāvaṇa.
t.5.1.37: If I do not see her, the daughter of Janaka, in Laṅkā, then with this very speed I shall go to the abode of the gods.
t.5.1.38: Or if, having made every effort, I do not find Sītā even in heaven, I shall bind Rāvaṇa, the king of the rākṣasas, and bring him back.
t.5.1.39: In every way I shall return having accomplished my task, coming back together with Sītā; or else, uprooting Laṅkā together with Rāvaṇa, I shall bring it here.
t.5.1.40: Having spoken thus to the monkeys, Hanumān, the foremost of monkeys, swift and without hesitation, then leapt up with great speed.
t.5.1.41: As he sprang up with great force, those trees growing on the mountain, drawing together all their branches, flew up on every side.
t.5.1.43: Uprooted by the force of his thighs, the trees followed the monkey for a moment, as kinsmen follow their own kinsman setting out on a long journey.
t.5.1.42: Sweeping along with the force of his thighs the excited koyaṣṭibhaka birds and the trees laden with flowers, he went on through the clear sky.
t.5.1.44: Uprooted by the force of his thighs, sāla trees and other excellent trees followed Hanumān, as soldiers follow their king.
t.5.1.45: Followed by many trees whose tops were richly in bloom, the monkey Hanumān, vast as a mountain, became a wondrous sight to behold.
t.5.1.46: Then those trees that were heavy sank into the salt water, just as the mountains, as if out of fear of the great Indra, had sunk into the abode of Varuṇa.
t.5.1.47: That monkey, resembling a cloud and strewn with many kinds of flowers along with sprouts and buds, shone like a mountain glittering with fireflies.
t.5.1.48: Released by his momentum, those trees, letting fall their flowers, sank down into the water, like friends who have turned back.
t.5.1.49: Being light, those many-hued, varied flowers of the trees, driven along by the wind of the monkey's flight, fell into the ocean.
t.5.1.50: With the many-hued mass of flowers clinging to him, the monkey shone like a rising cloud adorned with clusters of lightning.
t.5.1.51: With the flowers stirred up by the force of his speed, the water looked like the sky with lovely stars that have risen.
t.5.1.52: His two arms, stretched out as they moved through the sky, were seen like two five-mouthed serpents issuing forth from a mountain's summit.
t.5.1.54: As he followed the path of the wind, his two eyes, gleaming like lightning, blazed forth like two fires set upon a mountain.
t.5.1.53: The great monkey shone as if he were drinking up the mighty ocean with its network of waves, and he appeared as though he thirsted to drink the sky as well.
t.5.1.55: The two eyes of the foremost of the tawny-eyed ones, tawny, large and perfectly round, shone brilliantly like the moon and the sun set side by side.
t.5.1.56: His face, coppery red with its copper-colored nose, shone like the orb of the sun touched by the glow of twilight.
t.5.1.57: And the curled-up tail of the son of Vāyu, as he flew through the sky, shone like the raised banner of Śakra.
t.5.1.58: With the circle of his tail, the great and supremely wise son of Anila, white of fang, shone forth like the sun encircled by its halo.
t.5.1.59: With his deep red hindquarters that great monkey shone, like a mountain with a vast, split-open vein of red ochre.
t.5.1.60: As that lion among monkeys leapt across the ocean, the wind caught in the hollows of his armpits roared like a thundercloud.
t.5.1.61: Just as a meteor, issuing from the northern quarter, falls through the sky and is seen with its trailing tail, so did that elephant among monkeys appear.
t.5.1.62: Stretched out at full length and resembling a bird in flight, the monkey shone like a mighty full-grown elephant being bound with a girth.
t.5.1.63: With his body above and his shadow plunged into the ocean, the monkey then looked like a ship on the sea driven by the wind.
t.5.1.64: Whatever region of the ocean that great monkey passed over, that very region, stirred by the force of his body, appeared as if seized with frenzy.
t.5.1.66: The mighty wind raised by the monkey and the wind that issued from the clouds together violently shook the ocean, whose roar was terrible.
t.5.1.65: Striking with his chest the ocean's masses of waves, each as huge as a mountain, that great monkey of tremendous speed flew onward.
t.5.1.67: Dragging along the vast masses of waves in the salt sea, he of great speed passed beyond them, as if counting the billows.
t.5.1.68: Then the serpents dwelling in the ocean, beholding that tiger among monkeys leaping through the sky, took him to be Suparṇa.
t.5.1.69: Ten yojanas wide and thirty yojanas long, the shadow of that lion among monkeys upon the water became exceedingly beautiful.
t.5.1.70: His shadow, following the son of Vāyu and spread out upon the salt sea, shone like a long bank of white clouds.
t.5.1.71: Then, seeing that monkey leaping swiftly across, the Devas, Gandharvas and Dānavas rained down showers of flowers.
t.5.1.72: The sun did not scorch him, the lord of the monkeys, as he leapt across, and the wind then attended upon him for the accomplishment of Rāma's mission.
t.5.1.73: The ṛṣis praised him as he flew through the sky, and the devas and gandharvas sang, extolling the one of mighty energy.
t.5.1.74: And the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, gods and birds sang his praises, beholding in the sky that best of monkeys, suddenly freed from weariness.
t.5.1.75: While Hanūmān, that tiger among monkeys, was leaping through the sky, the Ocean, desiring to honour the race of Ikṣvāku, reflected thus.
t.5.1.76: If I do not render assistance to Hanumān, lord of the monkeys, I shall become an object of every reproach among those who wish to speak.
t.5.1.77: I was made to grow by Sagara, lord of the Ikṣvākus, and this one is a counsellor of the Ikṣvākus; he ought not to suffer distress.
t.5.1.78: I must act in such a way that the monkey may rest; and having rested on me, he will easily fly across the remaining distance.
t.5.1.79: Having thus formed this noble resolve, the Ocean spoke to Maināka, the golden-navelled, the best of mountains, who lay hidden in the waters.
t.5.1.80: O best of mountains, you were placed here by the king of the gods as a barrier against the hosts of Asuras who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
t.5.1.82: O mountain, you have the power to grow sideways, upward and downward as well; therefore I urge you: rise up, O best of mountains!
t.5.1.81: You stand covering the gateway of immeasurable Pātāla, barring these beings of known prowess, who would otherwise rise up once again.
t.5.1.83: This tiger among monkeys, the valiant Hanūmān of terrible deeds, has leapt into the sky for the sake of Rāma's mission and is passing above you.
t.5.1.84: Help must be given by me to him, who belongs to the line of Ikṣvāku. The Ikṣvākus are worthy of my reverence, and supremely worthy of yours.
t.5.1.85: Render us your assistance; let our duty not be neglected. A duty that ought to be done, if left undone, would rouse the anger of the virtuous.
t.5.1.88: Considering the compassion of Kākutstha, the banishment of Maithilī, and the toil of the lord of monkeys, you ought to rise up.
t.5.1.86: Rise up above the water, and let this monkey rest upon you. He is indeed our guest, and worthy of honor, the best of leapers.
t.5.1.87: O you of great golden peaks, frequented by gods and Gandharvas, Hanumān, having rested upon you, will then travel the rest of the way.
t.5.1.90: Then, bursting through the waters of the ocean, he rose up very high, just as the sun with blazing rays bursts through a cloud.
t.5.1.89: Hearing the words of the salt-watered ocean, Maināka, the golden-naveled mountain, swiftly rose up out of the water, covered with great trees and creepers.
t.5.1.91: With its golden peaks, home to Kiṃnaras and great serpents, gleaming like the rising sun and seeming to scrape the sky.
t.5.1.93: With its golden peaks, gleaming and radiant with their own light, that best of mountains became like a hundred suns.
t.5.1.92: By the golden peaks of that mountain rising up, the sky, which had been the colour of a sword-blade, became radiant with a golden glow.
t.5.1.94: Seeing it risen up unimpeded and standing before him in the midst of the salt sea, Hanumān was certain: “This is an obstacle.”
t.5.1.95: That great monkey of mighty speed struck down with his chest that exceedingly lofty one, as the wind brings down a cloud.
t.5.1.96: Then that best of mountains, pressed down by that monkey, perceiving the monkey's speed, was thrilled and rejoiced.
t.5.1.97: Pleased and glad at heart, the mountain, taking on a human form and standing upon its own peak, spoke these words to the heroic monkey, who had gone up into the sky and stood poised there in the air.
t.5.1.98: You have accomplished this difficult deed, O best of vānaras; alight upon my peaks and rest as you please.
t.5.1.99: The ocean was made to grow by those born in the lineage of Rāghava; therefore Sāgara honours you in return, you who are engaged in the welfare of Rāma.
t.5.1.100: When a good deed has been done, it must be repaid; this is the eternal dharma. He, desiring to repay that kindness, deserves honor from you.
t.5.1.101: On your account I have been urged by him out of great regard: “This monkey has leapt across a hundred yojanas; having rested upon your peaks, let him go on for the rest of the way.”
t.5.1.102: Stay, O tiger among monkeys; rest upon me and then go on. Here are fragrant, sweet bulbs, roots and fruits in plenty; having tasted them, O best of monkeys, you will continue on your way refreshed.
t.5.1.103: We too have a bond with you, O chief among monkeys, as all who dwell in the three worlds well know, a bond founded on the embrace of great virtues.
t.5.1.104: O son of Māruta, of all the swift monkeys who leap through the air, I consider you the very foremost, O elephant among monkeys.
t.5.1.105: A guest, even an ordinary one, is surely worthy of honour from one who is wise and seeks to know dharma; how much more so one such as you!
t.5.1.107: When you are honored, O knower of dharma, Māruta receives honor. Therefore you are worthy of honor from me; and hear also the reason for this.
t.5.1.106: For you, O elephant among monkeys, are the son of the great-souled Māruta, foremost among the gods, and you are equal to him in speed.
t.5.1.108: Long ago, in the Kṛta Age, dear one, the mountains had wings; they too flew in all directions, swift as Garuḍa and the wind.
t.5.1.109: Then, as they went flying off, the hosts of gods together with the sages, and all beings, became afraid, fearing that they would fall.
t.5.1.110: Then the thousand-eyed Śatakratu, enraged, cut off the wings of the mountains with his thunderbolt, here and there, by the thousands.
t.5.1.111: The king of the gods, enraged, came at me with his vajra raised; then I was suddenly hurled away by the great-souled Wind.
t.5.1.112: O best of monkeys, it was your father who cast me into this salt water and guarded me, so that my wings were kept safe and I remained whole.
t.5.1.113: Therefore I honour you, for Māruta is worthy of honour to me. Indeed, O chief of monkeys, this bond of mine with you is of great virtue.
t.5.1.114: Now that this matter has come to such a pass, O great monkey, you, with a gladdened heart, ought to give joy to the Ocean and to me as well.
t.5.1.116: Thus addressed, the best of monkeys said to that finest of mountains: "I am pleased; your hospitality is as good as done. Let this distress of yours be set aside."
t.5.1.115: Rid yourself of your weariness and accept my homage, O best of monkeys. Value highly my affection, for I am delighted at the sight of you.
t.5.1.117: The time for my task presses on me, and the day too is slipping past; a promise has been given by me, so I must not halt here midway.
t.5.1.118: Having spoken thus, the bull among monkeys touched the mountain with his hand; then the mighty one entered the sky and went on his way, as if smiling.
t.5.1.119: The son of Anila, regarded with great esteem by the mountain and the ocean, was honoured with fitting blessings.
t.5.1.120: Then, leaping far up into the air and leaving behind both the mountain and the great ocean, he took to his father's path and went on through the clear sky.
t.5.1.121: And again, having attained an upward course, the son of Vāyu, looking down upon that mountain, went on through the clear sky that offers no support.
t.5.1.122: Seeing that second, exceedingly difficult feat of Hanumān, all the gods, the Siddhas and the supreme seers praised him.
t.5.1.124: Then wise Śacīpati himself, out of deep satisfaction, spoke words choked with emotion to Sunābha, the foremost of mountains.
t.5.1.123: The deities stationed there were delighted by the deed of that golden Sunābha, and so too was the thousand-eyed Vāsava.
t.5.1.125: O Hiraṇyanābha, lord of mountains, I am greatly pleased with you. I grant you freedom from fear; remain, gentle one, as you please.
t.5.1.126: A very great help has been rendered by you to the valiant Hanumān, who was crossing a hundred yojanas, fearless even though there was cause for fear.
t.5.1.128: Then the best of mountains attained great joy, having seen Śatakratu, the lord of the gods, well pleased.
t.5.1.127: For this monkey goes on the mission of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; you have offered hospitality to the best of your power, and I am deeply pleased with you.
t.5.1.130: Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas and the supreme seers, spoke to Surasā, the mother of the Nāgas, who shone like the sun.
t.5.1.129: Then that mountain, having been granted a boon, stood firmly in its place, and Hanumān in a moment passed on across the ocean.
t.5.1.131: This glorious son of the Wind, Hanūmān by name, is leaping over the ocean. Create an obstacle for him for a moment.
t.5.1.132: Assuming a rākṣasa form, exceedingly dreadful and like a mountain, frightful with fangs and tawny-eyed, she made her mouth so vast that it touched the sky.
t.5.1.133: We wish to know his strength, and further his prowess: either he will overcome you by some stratagem, or he will fall into despair.
t.5.1.134: Thus addressed and duly honored by the deities, the goddess Surasā, in the midst of the ocean, assumed the form of a rākṣasī.
t.5.1.136: O bull among vānaras, you have been appointed by the lords as my food. I shall devour you; enter this mouth of mine.
t.5.1.135: Assuming a form that was distorted, hideous, and terrifying to all, she blocked the path of Hanūmān as he flew onward and spoke these words.
t.5.1.137: Thus addressed by Surasā, the glorious bull among monkeys, his hands joined in reverence and his face beaming with joy, spoke these words.
t.5.1.138: Rāma by name, the son of Daśaratha, entered the Daṇḍaka forest together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and also with his wife Vaidehī.
t.5.1.139: While he was intent upon his duty and had become bound in enmity with the Rākṣasas, his illustrious wife Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa.
t.5.1.140: As a messenger, at the command of Rāma, I shall go into her presence. O dweller in this realm, you ought to render aid to Rāma.
t.5.1.141: Or else, after I have seen Maithilī and Rāma, whose deeds are done without strain, I will come back into your mouth; I promise you this truly.
t.5.1.142: Thus addressed by Hanumān, Surasā, who could assume any form at will, said: "No one may pass beyond me; this is my boon."
t.5.1.143: Thus addressed by Surasā, the bull among monkeys grew angry and said, "Then make your mouth wide enough that you can bear me."
t.5.1.144: Having thus spoken to Surasā, the enraged Hanumān then became ten yojanas long and ten yojanas wide.
t.5.1.145: Seeing him, resembling a cloud and stretched out ten yojanas in length, Surasā too made her mouth twenty yojanas wide.
t.5.1.147: The heroic Hanumān became fifty yojanas tall; Surasā made her mouth sixty yojanas wide.
t.5.1.146: Then Hanumān, enraged, stretched himself out to a length of thirty yojanas, and Surasā in turn made her mouth forty yojanas high.
t.5.1.148: Even so the heroic Hanumān rose seventy yojanas high, and Surasā made her mouth eighty yojanas wide.
t.5.1.149: Hanūmān, resembling a mountain, rose ninety yojanas high; Surasā made her mouth a hundred yojanas wide.
t.5.1.150: But the wise son of Vāyu, seeing that mouth opened wide by Surasā, with its long tongue, most dreadful and like unto hell,
t.5.1.151: Contracting his own body like a cloud, that son of Māruta, Hanumān, became in that very moment no bigger than a thumb.
t.5.1.152: Swiftly darting into that mouth and darting out again, he of great speed, the glorious one, stood in the sky and spoke these words.
t.5.1.154: Seeing him freed from her mouth like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu, the goddess Surasā, in her own form, spoke to the monkey.
t.5.1.153: I have indeed entered your mouth, O Dākṣāyaṇī; salutations to you! I shall go where Vaidehī is, and may your word also prove true.
t.5.1.155: Go as you please, O best of monkeys, gentle one, for the accomplishment of your purpose, and unite Vaidehī with the great-souled Rāghava.
t.5.1.156: Seeing that third, exceedingly difficult feat of Hanumān, all beings then praised the monkey, crying, "Well done, well done!"
t.5.1.157: Having approached the ocean, the unassailable abode of Varuṇa, he entered the sky and went on with great speed, like Garuḍa.
t.5.1.158: Through the sky, served by the water-bearing clouds and frequented by birds, traversed by the masters of the Kaiśika art of music, and resorted to by Airāvata.
t.5.1.159: In the sky, which was splendidly adorned with spotless celestial chariots flying about, drawn by lions, elephants, tigers, birds and serpents.
t.5.1.160: He sped through the sky, which was lit up by fires striking like thunderbolts and lightning, and adorned with illustrious beings of meritorious deeds who had won heaven.
t.5.1.161: Through the sky, ever frequented by Citrabhānu as he bears the oblations, and adorned with planets, lunar mansions, the moon, the sun and hosts of stars.
t.5.1.162: Through the vast, open and spotless expanse, crowded with hosts of great Ṛṣis, Gandharvas, Nāgas and Yakṣas, and frequented by Viśvāvasu.
t.5.1.164: In that sky, often frequented by heroes and by excellent hosts of Vidyādharas, the great clouds shone brightly as they were drawn along by the monkey.
t.5.1.163: He moved through the auspicious path of the moon and the sun, trodden by the elephant of the king of the gods, the wide canopy fashioned by Brahmā and spread out over the world of living beings.
t.5.1.165: Entering the masses of clouds and emerging from them again and again, he then shone like the moon in the rainy season, now emerging, now entering.
t.5.1.166: But seeing him flying along, a rākṣasī named Siṃhikā, huge in size and able to take any form at will, reflected thus in her mind.
t.5.1.167: Today, after a long time, I shall be fed to my fill, for this great creature has at last, after long, come into my power.
t.5.1.169: I have been suddenly seized and held back, my strength rendered lame, like a great ship on the ocean by a contrary wind.
t.5.1.168: Having thus reflected in her mind, she seized his shadow. When his shadow had been seized, the monkey began to ponder.
t.5.1.170: Then the monkey, looking sideways, upward and downward, saw a mighty creature risen up from the salt sea.
t.5.1.171: That creature of wondrous appearance, the shadow-seizer of great might, of which the king of the monkeys spoke, is this very one; of this there is no doubt.
t.5.1.172: Having recognized her truly as Siṃhikā, the wise monkey, mighty of body, grew in size like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
t.5.1.173: Seeing the body of that great monkey growing larger, she stretched open her mouth, which was like the netherworld and the sky.
t.5.1.174: Then the wise and mighty monkey saw her hideous, enormous mouth, the full measure of her body, and her vital points.
t.5.1.176: The Siddhas and Cāraṇas saw him sinking into her mouth, like the full moon being swallowed by Rāhu at the time of the parvan.
t.5.1.175: That mighty monkey, whose frame was hard as a thunderbolt, contracted himself in an instant and plunged into her gaping mouth.
t.5.1.178: Seeing Siṃhikā slain by the monkey and quickly fallen, the beings that move through the sky spoke to that bull among leapers.
t.5.1.177: Then the monkey, tearing out its vitals with his sharp nails, sprang up with great speed, his stride as swift as the flight of the mind.
t.5.1.179: A fearsome deed has been done by you today, and a mighty creature has been slain by you. Accomplish your intended purpose unharmed, O best of leapers.
t.5.1.180: O lord of monkeys, whoever possesses these four qualities as you do, namely steadfastness, vision, wisdom and skill, never falters in his undertakings.
t.5.1.182: Having reached nearly the far shore, and looking about on every side, he beheld, at the end of a hundred yojanas, a line of forest.
t.5.1.181: Honored by them, the monkey, himself worthy of honor and intent on his purpose, entered the sky and went on like the devourer of serpents.
t.5.1.183: And even as he was still flying, the best of the monkeys saw the island adorned with many kinds of trees, and the groves of Malaya.
t.5.1.184: Gazing upon the ocean, upon the marshy shorelands of the ocean, upon the trees growing in those coastal lands, and even upon the mouths of the ocean's wives, the rivers.
t.5.1.185: Beholding himself, resembling a great cloud, as though obstructing the sky by his own self, the wise one made up his mind.
t.5.1.186: "On merely seeing the growth of my body and my great speed, the Rākṣasas would become curious about me," thus thought the great monkey.
t.5.1.187: Then, contracting that body which resembled a mountain, he returned once more to his natural form, like a self-possessed man whose delusion has passed away.
t.5.1.188: Having reached the far shore of the ocean, he, who could assume charming forms of many kinds and whose form could not be made out by others, looked himself over and carefully weighed his purpose.
t.5.1.190: Having by his strength crossed the ocean, filled with Dānavas and serpents and garlanded with mighty waves, and having alighted on the shore of the great sea, he then beheld Laṅkā, like Amarāvatī.
t.5.1.189: Then that great-souled one, who resembled the peak of a mighty mountain, alighted upon a rich, wondrously variegated peak of Mount Lamba, covered with ketaka, uddālaka and coconut trees.
